story: This prospective cohort study followed 183 people in China with kidney tumours (angiomyolipomas) from tuberous sclerosis complex. Everolimus shrank the tumours by half or more in 44% of patients at 3 months and 83% at 6 months, and fat-poor tumours responded better than fat-rich ones. A smaller dose looked similar in an exploratory, non-randomised comparison, so that point needs a randomised trial.
Ke Gao is first author. PubMed lists him in the Department of Urology at Xi'an People's Hospital.

highlights.GAO2026B: First author of the multicenter cohort study.

studies.title: Tumor fat composition predicts response to everolimus and supports low-dose therapy in TSC-associated renal angiomyolipomas: a multicenter prospective study
studies.finding: In a multicenter prospective cohort of 183 TSC-associated renal angiomyolipoma patients, everolimus reduced tumor volume by >=50% in 44% of patients at 3 months and 83% at 6 months; fat-poor lesions responded significantly better than fat-rich ones. No significant difference in response was detected between the low-dose and standard-dose groups in an exploratory, non-randomised subset, and oral mucositis was less frequent on the low dose; tumor regrowth occurred after treatment discontinuation.

story: In the Atlas, Nancy L Nadon is a middle author on 5 papers from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program, which tests whether drugs lengthen life in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Together they show that rapamycin extended lifespan in mice, with a bigger effect in females and at higher doses, that acarbose helped mainly males, and that resveratrol, simvastatin and several other popular compounds did not change lifespan. All of this is mouse work.

PubMed lists no affiliation for Nancy L Nadon in these records. A 2016 paper from the same program, sharing several co-authors, lists her at the Division of Aging Biology, National Institute on Aging, in Bethesda, Maryland.

story: Anurag Saxena was first author of the 2026 TRON trial in the Atlas, with Julian R. Sampson as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Division of Cancer and Genetics, School of Medicine, Cardiff University.

The multicentre trial randomised 38 people with tuberous sclerosis complex, two to one, to everolimus or placebo for 24 weeks. Similar shares of people improved on thinking tests with the drug and with placebo (87% and 75%), which points to strong practice or placebo effects rather than a clear benefit for cognition.

studies.title: Everolimus for the treatment of neuropsychological deficits in tuberous sclerosis complex: findings from the TRON multicentre randomised controlled trial
studies.finding: In a multicentre RCT of TSC patients (n=38 randomised, 2:1 everolimus:placebo), 24 weeks of everolimus produced similarly large 'responder' rates for neuropsychological improvement as placebo (87% vs 75%), suggesting large practice/placebo effects rather than a clear drug benefit on cognition -- despite everolimus's established efficacy for TSC tumours and epilepsy. story: Petrus J de Vries is a middle author on two human trials in the Atlas, both in people with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), a genetic condition in which mTOR is switched on too much. The TRON trial (2026) looked at thinking and behaviour in 38 people. Everolimus did not clearly beat placebo there, because both groups improved a lot. Two other EXIST papers in the Atlas list the same name, but their PubMed records give no affiliation, so they are not covered here.

studies.title: Efficacy and safety of sirolimus in lymphangioleiomyomatosis (MILES)
studies.finding:
MILES was a 12-month placebo-controlled trial of sirolimus in 89 women with lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a rare lung disease driven by overactive mTOR. On placebo, lung function (FEV1) fell by about 12 ml a month. On sirolimus it held steady (+1 ml a month), a 153 ml difference over the year. In the next year nobody took the drug, and the sirolimus group's decline resumed in parallel with placebo, so the benefit lasted only while the drug was taken. Walking distance and gas-transfer capacity did not improve.

studies.finding: An integrated high-throughput lifespan-screening platform spanning yeast, nematodes, flies, killifish and mice, evaluating >400 compounds across thousands of conditions using automated imaging and deep-learning death detection. Cross-species integration identifies geroprotectors active in multiple species and shows convergence on known and novel conserved longevity pathways. Methodological infrastructure for the question the Atlas keeps running into: which single-species lifespan results actually generalise. Note the abstract does not name individual hit compounds, so the specific standing of rapamycin/mTOR in this screen cannot be read off the abstract alone.

studies.finding: mTOR is a key regulator of memory CD8 T-cell differentiation; rapamycin enhances memory responses.

current.lab_name: Epilepsy Research Program, School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences, University of South Australia (Adelaide, South Australia, Australia)
current.role: First author of the 2013 Nature Genetics study linking DEPDC5 mutations to familial focal epilepsy.
current.sub: Epilepsy Research Program · University of South Australia · Adelaide, Australia
story: Leanne M Dibbens is first author of a 2013 paper in Nature Genetics. Using exome sequencing in families with focal epilepsy, the team found loss-of-function mutations in DEPDC5, which codes for a part of the GATOR1 complex. They found these mutations in 5 of 6 further published large families and in about 12% (10 of 82) of smaller families. This is human genetic evidence that GATOR1 matters for brain function. PubMed lists her at the University of South Australia.

highlights.DIB2013B: First author of the study that found DEPDC5 mutations in familial focal epilepsy.

pubmed_affiliation: Epilepsy Research Program, School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences, University of South Australia, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia.

studies.title: Mutations in DEPDC5 cause familial focal epilepsy with variable foci
studies.finding: Exome sequencing and linkage in families with autosomal dominant familial focal epilepsy with variable foci identified loss-of-function mutations in DEPDC5, a GATOR1 subunit, in 5 of 6 additional published large families and in roughly 12% (10/82) of smaller focal-epilepsy families. This is the human genetic anchor for GATOR1's physiological importance: it supports that loss of a GATOR1 subunit produces a human phenotype. Observational genetic association within families, not an interventional study, and the paper carries no mTORC1 readout of its own - the link to the pathway rests on the molecular work (BAR2013, SHE2018), not on this study.

current.sub: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Grenoble Outstation, France
story: Manikandan Karuppasamy is first author of an Atlas study (KAR2017) that used electron cryo-microscopy to determine the structure of TORC2 from baker's yeast. The complex has six subunits. Its Avo3 (Rictor) part covers the site where the FKBP12-rapamycin drug complex would attach, which helps explain why TORC2 resists rapamycin. PubMed lists Karuppasamy at the EMBL Grenoble Outstation.

highlights.KAR2017: First author: reported the cryo-EM structure of yeast TORC2 and what it shows about rapamycin insensitivity.

pubmed_affiliation: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Grenoble Outstation, 71 Avenue des Martyrs, 38042, Grenoble, France.

studies.title: Cryo-EM structure of Saccharomyces cerevisiae target of rapamycin complex 2
studies.finding: Cryo-EM structure of yeast TORC2 reveals its overall architecture and rapamycin insensitivity.

current.lab_name: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University (Aarhus, Denmark)
current.role: First author of a 2026 ex vivo mouse muscle study on mTORC1 and JNK-SMAD2L responses to stretch in young and old muscle.
current.sub: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University, Denmark
story: Jonas Boritz Kristiansen is first author of an Atlas study (KRISTIANSEN2026) on muscle from adult and 24-month-old female mice, kept alive outside the body. A standard passive stretch raised mTORC1 signaling to a similar degree in both age groups. The JNK-SMAD2L response to the same stretch was weaker in old muscle. The authors read this as mTORC1 mechanosensing being preserved with age in this model. PubMed lists Kristiansen at Aarhus University.

highlights.KRISTIANSEN2026: First author: reported that stretch-induced mTORC1 signaling is preserved in old mouse muscle while JNK-SMAD2L signaling is blunted.

pubmed_affiliation: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark.

studies.title: Aging preserves mTORC1 but attenuates JNK-SMAD2L signaling sensitivity to passive stretch-induced tension development in isolated mouse skeletal muscle.
studies.finding: Passive mechanical stretch activated mTORC1 signalling (mTOR, p70S6K, rpS6, 4E-BP1) to a similar degree in ex vivo muscle from adult and old female mice, whereas JNK-SMAD2L activation by the same stretch was blunted with age, suggesting mTORC1 mechanosensitivity itself is preserved in this model.
